docs.title: Research Methods in the Age of AI
Graduate research methods for an AI-mediated world
docs.text:
This course combines traditional research methodology with contemporary computational tools, including Python, Google Colab, pretrained language models, and generative AI.

The course focuses on how researchers move from research questions to evidence: reviewing literature, selecting appropriate research designs, collecting and organizing data, analyzing results, evaluating AI-assisted workflows, and communicating findings.

Tools can assist research, but they cannot replace methodological judgment.

View the syllabus Explore the weekly schedule

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
• Design Research

Develop research questions and hypotheses, evaluate scholarly evidence, and select appropriate sampling, measurement, survey, experimental, and quasi-experimental designs.

  • Analyze Data

Prepare, analyze, and interpret quantitative data using introductory statistical methods and reproducible Python workflows in Google Colab.

  • Work with AI

Use large language models and pretrained language models as research tools while learning how to evaluate their outputs, limitations, and appropriate uses.

  • Maintain Human Oversight

Verify analytical and AI-generated outputs, examine errors and limitations, protect sensitive information, and make defensible research decisions.

docs.title: Block 1 — Modern Research Tools in the Age of AI
docs.text:
Begin by examining how research is changing as AI, computation, and large language models become part of contemporary research workflows.

You will learn foundational concepts behind large language models and Transformers, become familiar with Google Colab and basic Python, and explore how pretrained language models can support research tasks such as literature screening and classification.

The goal is computational literacy, not software engineering. No prior programming experience is required.

docs.title: Block 2 — Data Collection and Research Design
docs.text:
Move from tools to research decisions.

You will learn how research questions connect to sampling, measurement, surveys, randomized experiments, A/B testing, and quasi-experimental designs. Emphasis is placed on selecting and justifying a research design that provides appropriate evidence for the question being asked.

docs.title: Block 3 — Data Analysis and Interpretation
docs.text:
Learn how research data are organized, prepared, analyzed, and interpreted.

You will work with data cleaning and introductory analytical approaches including correlation, t-tests, linear regression, analysis of variance, chi-square, and computational text and sentiment classification.

Most topics follow a concept → guided application structure, with greater emphasis on analytical reasoning and interpretation than on extensive programming.

docs.title: Block 4 — Responsible Research and Communication
docs.text:
Bring the research process together through responsible analysis and communication.

You will consider AI ethics, reproducibility, limitations, appropriate human oversight, and the communication of analytical findings to academic, industry, technology, nonprofit, and other stakeholder audiences.

The course concludes with a group research project in which you will apply an appropriate analytical approach to an instructor-provided dataset and communicate what the evidence means.

docs.title: Course Format
docs.text:
The course is taught primarily through in-person concept sessions and selected synchronous computational laboratories.

A small number of laboratory sessions use Zoom when the digital environment provides specific instructional advantages, including screen sharing, live debugging, Google Colab demonstrations, and collaborative examination of computational workflows.

Session Type Primary Focus Concept sessions Research logic, design, interpretation, discussion, and methodological decision-making Computational laboratories Python, Google Colab, AI tools, data analysis, screen sharing, and live debugging Workshops Research design, analytical planning, interpretation, and stakeholder communication

docs.title: Course Tools
docs.text:
You will work with several contemporary research tools throughout the course:

  • Google Colab for browser-based Python notebooks
  • Python for introductory data management, analysis, and computational research
  • Pretrained language models for guided language-processing activities
  • Generative AI for selected research and coding activities
  • GitHub for openly accessible instructional materials and reproducible course resources

You are not expected to memorize Python syntax or become an AI engineer. The emphasis is on understanding what the tools are doing, when they are appropriate, and how their outputs should be evaluated.

docs.title: Begin Here
docs.text:
1. Review the course syllabus.
  2. Examine the weekly schedule.
  3. Read the AI use policy.
  4. Open the lecture materials.

docs.title: Guiding Principle
docs.text: AI may assist your research and coding, but it may not replace your understanding, judgment, validation, or responsibility.

docs.title: Permitted Uses
docs.text:
You may use approved AI systems to:

  • request explanations of code;
  • generate an initial code structure;
  • create test cases;
  • compare analytical approaches;
  • improve code readability;
  • review code for potential mistakes; and
  • explore alternative visualizations.

docs.title: Your Responsibilities
docs.text:
You must be able to:

  1. explain what your code is intended to do;
  2. identify the data and variables used;
  3. interpret the output;
  4. explain how the output was verified;
  5. identify possible errors and limitations; and
  6. modify the analysis when the data or research question changes.

docs.title: Required AI Documentation
docs.text:
For major assignments, you may be asked to document:

  • which AI tools you used;
  • what you asked the tools to do;
  • representative prompts or instructions;
  • what you changed; and
  • how you checked the outputs.

docs.title: Data Privacy
docs.text:
Do not upload any of the following to an external AI system:

  • personally identifiable information;
  • private or confidential information;
  • protected research-participant data;
  • proprietary datasets;
  • authentication credentials; or
  • API keys.

Never publish API keys

API keys must never appear in a notebook, public repository, screenshot,
lecture slide, or assignment submission.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
Research methods are changing as computation, large language models, and increasingly accessible analytical tools become part of everyday research.

In this course, you will learn how to move from a research question to evidence: reviewing literature, selecting appropriate research designs, organizing and analyzing data, interpreting findings, evaluating AI-assisted workflows, and communicating results.

The course combines traditional research methodology with modern research tools, including Python, Google Colab, pretrained language models, and generative AI. Programming is treated as a research tool rather than as an end in itself. No prior programming experience is required.

Tools can assist research, but they cannot replace methodological judgment.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text: By the end of the course, you should be able to:

docs.title: Overall Research Competency
docs.text: 1. Explain the major stages of the research process and connect research questions to evidence, research design, data analysis, interpretation, and communication of findings.

docs.title: Block 1 — Modern Research Tools in the Age of AI
docs.text:
1. Explain foundational concepts behind contemporary AI and large language models at a level relevant to research.
  2. Use Google Colab and basic Python to support reproducible research tasks.
  3. Critically evaluate the capabilities, limitations, and appropriate uses of AI and pretrained language models in research workflows.

docs.title: Block 2 — Data Collection and Research Design
docs.text:
1. Develop research questions and hypotheses grounded in scholarly literature.
  2. Distinguish among major quantitative research designs, including surveys, experiments, A/B tests, and quasi-experiments.
  3. Identify and justify appropriate sampling, measurement, and data-collection strategies.

docs.title: Block 3 — Data Analysis and Interpretation
docs.text:
1. Select and conduct introductory statistical analyses, including correlation, t-tests, regression, ANOVA, and chi-square.
  2. Apply introductory computational approaches to text data, including sentiment analysis or text classification.
  3. Interpret analytical results in substantive rather than purely statistical terms, recognizing relevant assumptions and limitations.

docs.title: Block 4 — Responsible Research and Communication
docs.text:
1. Identify ethical, validity, and reproducibility concerns associated with computational and AI-assisted research.
  2. Communicate research findings and their limitations to academic, industry, and other stakeholder audiences.

docs.title: Course Structure
docs.text:
The course is organized into four interconnected blocks that guide students from foundational computational literacy to research design, data analysis, and responsible communication of findings.

Because AI and computational tools are increasingly integrated into research practice, the course begins by introducing these tools and their capabilities and limitations. This foundation prepares students to evaluate when and how to use them throughout the research process.

docs.title: Block 1 — Modern Research Tools in the Age of AI
docs.text:
You will begin by examining how AI and computation are changing contemporary research. Topics include large language models, Transformer foundations, Google Colab, Python fundamentals, pretrained language models, and human evaluation of AI-assisted research workflows.

Through guided activities, you will compare human judgment with AI-assisted research tasks and learn to evaluate the capabilities, limitations, and appropriate uses of these tools.

The emphasis is on computational literacy and critical evaluation, not software engineering or memorizing programming syntax. This foundation prepares you to integrate computational tools thoughtfully into subsequent research activities.

docs.title: Block 2 — Data Collection and Research Design
docs.text:
Building on this foundation, you will move from understanding research tools to making methodological decisions.

Topics include research questions and hypotheses, sampling, measurement, surveys, randomized experiments, A/B testing, quasi-experimental designs, reliability, and validity.

You will learn to select and justify research designs based on the research question, recognizing that computational and AI tools can support—but cannot replace—sound methodological judgment.

docs.title: Block 3 — Data Analysis and Interpretation
docs.text:
You will apply your computational foundation and methodological knowledge to preparing, analyzing, and interpreting research data.

Topics include data cleaning, correlation, t-tests, linear regression, ANOVA, chi-square, and introductory computational text analysis and sentiment classification.

Most analytical topics follow a concept → guided application structure using Python and Google Colab.

The emphasis is on selecting appropriate analytical methods, interpreting findings, evaluating assumptions, and understanding limitations rather than extensive programming.

docs.title: Block 4 — Responsible Research and Communication
docs.text:
The final block brings together the knowledge and skills developed throughout the course.

You will integrate analytical reasoning with research ethics, responsible AI use, reproducibility, human oversight, research limitations, and stakeholder communication.

The course concludes with an applied group research project in which you use an instructor-provided dataset, select an appropriate analytical approach, interpret the results, and communicate what the evidence means.

docs.title: Technology
docs.text:
You will work with:

  • Google Colab for browser-based computational notebooks
  • Python for introductory data management and analysis
  • pandas and NumPy for working with structured data
  • SciPy and statsmodels for introductory statistical analysis
  • Matplotlib for data visualization
  • Pretrained language models for guided computational text activities
  • Generative AI for selected research and coding activities
  • GitHub for openly accessible instructional and computational materials

No prior programming experience is required.

You are not expected to memorize Python syntax or become an AI engineer. The emphasis is on understanding what computational tools are doing, when they are appropriate, and how their outputs should be evaluated.

docs.title: Course Readings
docs.text:
There is no required textbook to purchase.

Research methodology, computational tools, and AI are evolving quickly, and no single textbook adequately covers the full scope of the course.

Readings are therefore selected from freely available books, scholarly articles, technical documentation, and instructor-provided materials.

Specific required readings and preparation materials are communicated through the official course platform. Reading links and additional references are also organized by instructional block on this website.

You are not expected to read an entire technical book from beginning to end unless specifically assigned.

View course readings and resources

docs.title: Assessments
docs.text:
Assessments are aligned with the four instructional blocks.

Assessment Learning Focus Weight Colab Access Check Block 1: Computational Preparation 5% Human + AI Literature Screening Exercise Block 1: AI-Assisted Research and Critical Evaluation 15% Block 1 Knowledge Assessment Block 1: Computational and AI Literacy 20% Research Design Brief Block 2: Data Collection and Research Design 20% Final Project Analysis Plan Blocks 3–4: Analysis and Responsible Research 10% Final Stakeholder Research Presentation Blocks 3–4: Analysis, Interpretation, and Communication 30% Total 100%

The assessment sequence moves from understanding and evaluating modern research tools, to making research-design decisions, to conducting and communicating an applied analysis.

Early assignments emphasize computational literacy and critical evaluation of AI-assisted research workflows.

The Research Design Brief focuses on developing a coherent study grounded in scholarly literature and sound methodological decisions.

The final project integrates data analysis, interpretation, responsible research practices, and communication of findings to stakeholders.

docs.title: AI and Human Oversight
docs.text:
AI is intentionally incorporated into selected course activities.

You will learn to use AI systems as research tools whose outputs require evaluation, rather than as substitutes for independent research judgment.

Depending on the activity, AI may support:

  • Literature organization
  • Classification
  • Coding assistance
  • Debugging
  • Computational research workflows
  • Methodological critique

The specific tools and permitted uses may vary by activity or assignment.

You remain responsible for:

  • Verifying AI-generated information and code
  • Understanding the analyses you conduct
  • Identifying errors, biases, and limitations
  • Protecting sensitive information
  • Documenting AI use when required
  • Making independent methodological and interpretive decisions

AI use must follow the instructions for each assignment. Using AI to generate work that is required to be completed independently is not permitted.

The emphasis throughout the course is on human judgment, methodological reasoning, and responsible evaluation of computational tools.

docs.text:
These public pages provide an overview of the major learning activities and preparation materials for the course.

Assignment What You Do What It Demonstrates Colab Access Check Set up access to Google Colab and confirm that you can open and use a computational notebook. Readiness to work in a cloud-based research environment Human + AI Literature Screening Exercise Work with a research question, identify peer-reviewed studies, make your own relevance judgments, and compare those judgments with classifications produced by a pretrained language model. docs.title: Assignment Philosophy
docs.text:
The assignments are designed to move progressively from:

tool literacy → research design → analysis → interpretation and communication

Across the course, the emphasis is not simply on whether a computational or AI tool produces an answer. You should also be able to explain:

  • why a research approach is appropriate;
  • what the computational or AI tool is doing;
  • how you verified the output;
  • what limitations remain; and
  • what the evidence means for the research question.

docs.title: Week 3 Zoom Lab: Python Research Workflow
Exploring TikTok User Experiences with Python
docs.text:
Today, you will practice reading, running, modifying, and explaining simple Python code using data from a fictional TikTok user-experience study. The research context is new, but the core Python ideas are the ones introduced in class:

  • variables and =
  • text and quotation marks
  • print() and len()
  • lists and indexes
  • loops and indentation
  • if and in
  • string tools such as .lower()

The goal is not to memorize Python syntax or conduct a real content analysis. The goal is to understand what short pieces of code ask the computer to do and to check whether the output makes sense.

Today's Cycle

Predict → Run → Look → Explain → Modify

docs.title: The Research Story
docs.text:
Imagine that a research team wants to understand how college students experience TikTok. The researchers are especially interested in how students describe:

  • TikTok's recommendation algorithm
  • advertisements
  • discovering new creators
  • repetitive content
  • losing track of time while scrolling

The researchers ask students an open-ended survey question:

What do you like or dislike about your experience using TikTok?

Each student writes a short response. The research team now has many comments, such as:

The algorithm knows what I like.
There are too many ads now.
I like discovering new creators.
The For You page feels repetitive.
Sometimes I lose track of time while scrolling.

Reading a few comments by hand is easy. If the researchers collected hundreds or thousands of comments, however, they might use Python to help organize the comments, retrieve particular responses, repeat the same step for every response, and find comments containing specific words.

docs.title: Our Research Question
docs.text:
For this lab, we will ask:

How can Python help us organize and explore students' comments about their TikTok experiences?

Each group will practice one small part of that research workflow. No group will answer the entire research question alone. When the groups share their results, we will combine the pieces to see how a larger Python workflow is built.

Note

All comments and participant IDs in this lab are fictional and are used only to practice Python. Finding a word in a comment does not, by itself, tell us what all TikTok users think or whether an experience is positive or negative.

docs.title: How the Group Activity Works
docs.text: There are eight groups with approximately three students in each group. Each group will be assigned one task and will have approximately 10 minutes to work.

docs.title: Work Together—but Use Your Own Laptop
docs.text:
This is group work, but every student should complete the task in their own Google Colab notebook on their own laptop.

Group members should:

  1. read the task together
  2. discuss predictions before running the code
  3. help one another understand instructions and errors
  4. compare outputs
  5. discuss the AI-assisted modification
  6. make sure everyone can explain the code

Do not have only one person complete the code while everyone else watches. Everyone should type or copy, run, modify, and inspect the code independently.

docs.title: Suggested Use of Your 10 Minutes
docs.text:
• Minutes 1–2: Read the task and make predictions.
  • Minutes 3–6: Run and modify the code on each laptop.
  • Minutes 7–9: Complete the AI-assisted modification.
  • Minute 10: Decide what your group will explain to the class.

docs.title: When Your Group Shares
docs.text:
One group member may share a screen. Other members should be ready to help explain:

  1. what the task asked Python to do
  2. what the group predicted
  3. what code the group ran or changed
  4. what output appeared
  5. how the group checked the result
  6. what the group learned from the AI-assisted modification

docs.title: Using AI During the Lab
docs.text:
Each task ends with a small modification involving a Python idea that was not directly taught in class. You may use an approved AI assistant to help with that part.

Start with a prompt such as:

I am a Python beginner. Help me make the modification described below.
Use the simplest possible code and explain only the new part in plain English.
Do not change the parts of my code that already work.

Then add a Markdown cell to your notebook:

AI prompt I used:

New code AI suggested:

What the new code does:

How I verified the result:

Warning

AI-generated code is a proposed solution, not a verified solution. Run it, inspect the output, and decide whether it actually answers the question.

docs.title: Group 1: Store and Display a Comment
docs.text:
Copy this code into a code cell:

comment = "The Algorithm Knows What I Like"
print(comment)

docs.title: A. Predict and Explain
docs.text:
Before running the code, discuss:

  1. Which part is the variable name?
  2. What does = tell Python to do?
  3. Why does the comment need quotation marks?
  4. What do you predict will appear under the cell?

Run the code and check your prediction.

docs.title: B. Modify the Code
docs.text:
Change the stored comment to There Are Too Many Ads Now. Run the cell again and explain why the output changed.

Then create a second variable called participant that stores the text P07. Print both variables.

docs.title: C. AI-Assisted Modification: Print Both on One Line
docs.text:
Ask AI to show you the simplest way to print the participant ID and comment together on one line, separated by a hyphen.

Your intended output is:

P07 - There Are Too Many Ads Now

Run the suggestion and verify that both pieces of text appear in the correct order.

docs.title: Group 2: Retrieve Items from a List
docs.text:
Copy and run this code:

comments = [
    "The algorithm knows what I like",
    "There are too many ads now",
    "I like discovering new creators",
    "The For You page feels repetitive"
]

docs.title: A. Predict and Retrieve
docs.text:
Before running these lines, predict each output:

print(comments[0])
print(comments[1])
print(comments[2])

Run the code and check your predictions.

docs.title: B. Modify the Code
docs.text:
1. Write one line that prints the fourth comment.
  2. Change the second comment in the list to a comment of your choice.
  3. Run your retrieval code again and confirm that the new comment appears.

Complete this explanation:

comments[0] retrieves the __________ item because Python starts counting at __________.

docs.title: C. AI-Assisted Modification: Retrieve the Final Item Another Way
docs.text:
Ask AI whether Python can retrieve the final list item without first counting the items. Ask it to explain the new index in plain English.

Run the suggested code and verify that it returns the fourth comment.

docs.title: Group 3: Count Items in a List
docs.text:
Copy this code:

comments = [
    "The algorithm knows what I like",
    "There are too many ads now",
    "I like discovering new creators"
]

print(len(comments))

docs.title: A. Predict and Explain
docs.text:
Before running the code, discuss:

  1. What information is stored in comments?
  2. What action does len() perform?
  3. What output do you predict?

Run the code and check your prediction.

docs.title: B. Modify the Code
docs.text:
Add two new comments inside the square brackets. Run the code again.

Discuss:

  1. How and why did the output change?
  2. Does len() count from zero, or report the total number of items?

docs.title: C. AI-Assisted Modification: Add an Item with .append()
docs.text:
Ask AI how to use .append() to add this comment after the list has already been created:

Sometimes I lose track of time while scrolling

Print the list and its new length. Verify that the comment appears once and that the total increases by one.

docs.title: Group 4: Repeat an Instruction with a Loop
docs.text:
Copy this code:

comments = [
    "The algorithm knows what I like",
    "There are too many ads now",
    "I like discovering new creators"
]

for comment in comments:
    print(comment)

docs.title: A. Predict and Explain
docs.text:
Before running the code, discuss:

  1. How many lines of output do you predict?
  2. What does comment represent during each repetition?
  3. Why is print(comment) indented?

Run the code and check your prediction.

docs.title: B. Modify the Code
docs.text:
Add this unindented line after the loop:

print("Finished")

Run the code. Explain why each comment prints once but Finished prints only once.

Then temporarily remove the indentation before print(comment). Run the code, read the error, restore the indentation, and confirm that it works again.

docs.title: C. AI-Assisted Modification: Number the Comments
docs.text:
Ask AI for a beginner-friendly way to number the printed comments 1, 2, and 3. Ask it to explain only the new Python idea.

Run the suggestion. Verify that every comment still appears and that the displayed numbers begin with 1.

docs.title: Group 5: Use if to Make a Decision
docs.text:
Copy this code:

comment = "The algorithm knows what I like"

if "algorithm" in comment:
    print("This comment mentions the algorithm")

docs.title: A. Predict and Explain
docs.text:
Before running the code, discuss:

  1. What True/False question is Python checking?
  2. Do you expect the message to print?
  3. Why is the print() line indented?

Run the code and check your answers.

docs.title: B. Modify the Code
docs.text:
Change the stored comment to:

comment = "There are too many ads now"

Run the code again. Explain why no message appears.

Then change the condition so Python searches for ads. Run it and verify the result.

docs.title: C. AI-Assisted Modification: Add an else
docs.text:
Ask AI how to make Python print This comment does not mention the algorithm when the condition is not true. Ask it to use an else statement and explain how if and else work together.

Test the code with one comment that mentions the algorithm and one that does not. Verify that exactly one message appears for each comment.

docs.title: Group 6: Combine a List, Loop, and if
docs.text:
Copy this code:

comments = [
    "The algorithm knows what I like",
    "There are too many ads now",
    "I like discovering new creators",
    "The algorithm keeps recommending similar videos"
]

for comment in comments:
    if "algorithm" in comment:
        print(comment)

docs.title: A. Predict and Explain
docs.text:
Before running the code:

  1. Predict which comments will print.
  2. Identify the line that repeats.
  3. Identify the line that checks a condition.
  4. Explain why the final line has more indentation.

Run the code and compare the output with your prediction.

docs.title: B. Modify the Research Question
docs.text:
Change the code so it prints only comments containing creators. Then add this comment to the list:

I follow creators who explain new dance trends

Run the code again. Verify that the output answers the new question.

docs.title: C. AI-Assisted Modification: Count the Matches
docs.text:
Ask AI to modify the original algorithm-search code so it also counts how many comments contain algorithm. Ask it to use a simple counter and explain the new lines.

Run the suggestion. Verify the count by manually checking the four comments yourself.

docs.title: Group 7: Make a Search Ignore Capitalization
docs.text:
Copy this code:

comments = [
    "The algorithm knows what I like",
    "There are too many ads now",
    "The ALGORITHM recommends videos I enjoy"
]

for comment in comments:
    if "algorithm" in comment:
        print(comment)

docs.title: A. Predict and Investigate
docs.text:
Before running the code, predict whether Python will print both comments that discuss the algorithm.

Run the code and discuss:

  1. Which expected comment is missing?
  2. What difference do you notice between algorithm and ALGORITHM?
  3. Does Python treat uppercase and lowercase letters as identical here?

docs.title: B. Modify the Code
docs.text:
Use .lower() to make the search ignore capitalization:

for comment in comments:
    if "algorithm" in comment.lower():
        print(comment)

Run the code and verify that both relevant comments appear.

Complete this explanation:

The dot tells Python to use the __________ tool that belongs to the current __________.

docs.title: C. AI-Assisted Modification: Search for Two Possible Words
docs.text:
Ask AI to modify the condition so the code prints a comment when it contains either algorithm or ads, regardless of capitalization. Ask it to explain the word or.

Add another comment containing ads, run the code, and manually verify every match.

docs.title: Group 8: Debug and Verify a Small Workflow
docs.text:
This code should print only comments containing algorithm, but it has problems:

comments = [
    "The algorithm knows what I like",
    "There are too many ads now",
    "The algorithm keeps recommending similar videos"
]

for comment in comments
if "algorithm" in comment:
print(comment)

docs.title: A. Predict the Intended Result
docs.text:
Before running the code:

  1. Identify which comments should print if the code works.
  2. Identify the list, loop, condition, and action.

docs.title: B. Debug One Problem at a Time
docs.text:
Run the code and read the first error. Fix one problem, run the code again, and continue until the intended comments appear.

Keep a record in a Markdown cell:

Problem 1:
How we fixed it:

Problem 2:
How we fixed it:

How we verified the final output:

docs.title: C. AI-Assisted Modification: Request Hints, Not the Whole Answer
docs.text:
If your group becomes stuck, ask AI:

Explain the first remaining problem in this Python code.
Give me one hint, but do not rewrite the full solution.

After the code works, ask AI to add one final unindented line that reports Search finished. Verify that it appears once, after all matching comments.

docs.title: What You Practiced
docs.text:
By the end of the lab, the class should have practiced how to:

  • store text with variables
  • group text in lists
  • retrieve list items with indexes
  • count items with len()
  • repeat instructions with loops
  • use indentation to show which instructions repeat
  • use if and in to check a condition
  • use .lower() to make a search ignore capitalization
  • read and respond to simple errors
  • modify code for a slightly different research question
  • use AI to learn one small new Python idea
  • verify AI-generated code by inspecting the output

Note

Different groups will work with different Python ideas. During screen sharing, focus on understanding how each group translated its code into everyday language and verified its result.

docs.title: Week 4 Lab: Human + AI Literature Screening
What this lab is about
docs.text:
Today, your group will use the abstracts you already collected to ask one research-methods question:

Can an AI model help us decide which articles are relevant to our research question?

The goal is not to learn or memorize the Hugging Face or pandas code. The code is provided. Your job is to run it, inspect the output, compare it with human judgment, and decide when the AI is useful or wrong.

docs.title: Not required for the Block 1 exam
docs.text:
You do not need to memorize pipeline(), pandas/DataFrame commands, Hugging Face syntax, or the AI-classification code in this lab.

You should understand the research logic:

Research question → Human judgment → AI judgment → Compare → Validate

docs.title: 1. Start with the work your group already completed
docs.text:
Your group should already have:

  • One research question
  • 3 peer-reviewed article abstracts per person
  • About 12–15 abstracts total
  • One combined .csv file
  • At least these two columns: Group Member and abstract

Do not find a new set of abstracts for this lab.

docs.title: 2. Human judgment comes FIRST
docs.text:
Before running the AI model, return to the 3 abstracts you personally contributed.

For each abstract, privately choose one judgment:

  • Clearly relevant — directly helps answer your research question
  • Possibly relevant — related, but the connection is incomplete or uncertain
  • Probably unrelated — does not really help answer your research question

Write down your judgments before looking at the AI results. Do not change your original judgment after seeing the AI prediction.

docs.title: 3. Open Google Colab
docs.text: Open a new Google Colab notebook. You will copy and run the code below.

docs.title: Code A — Install and import the tools
docs.text:
Just run this cell. You do not need to memorize it.

!pip -q install transformers

import pandas as pd
from google.colab import files
from transformers import pipeline

In plain English: Get the tools we need.

docs.title: Code B — Upload and open your file
docs.text:
uploaded = files.upload()
filename = next(iter(uploaded))

df = pd.read_csv(filename)
df.columns = df.columns.str.strip()

df.head()

In plain English: Upload our file → open it as a table → show the first few rows.

Check that you can see your abstracts. Your file must contain a column named abstract.

docs.title: 5. Tell the notebook your research question
Code C — CHANGE ONLY the text between the quotation marks
docs.text:
research_question = "How does social media coverage influence fans' perceptions of athletes?"

print(research_question)

Replace the example with your group's research question. Keep the quotation marks.

docs.title: Code D — Just run this cell
docs.text:
classifier = pipeline(
    "zero-shot-classification",
    model="facebook/bart-large-mnli"
)

The first run may take a few minutes because Colab has to download the model.

In plain English: Load an existing model that can compare text with categories we provide.

docs.title: Code E — Create the three screening categories
docs.text:
candidate_labels = [
    f"clearly relevant to the research question: {research_question}",
    f"possibly relevant to the research question: {research_question}",
    f"probably unrelated to the research question: {research_question}"
]

docs.title: Code F — Ask the model about the first abstract
docs.text:
abstract = str(df.loc[0, "abstract"])

result = classifier(
    abstract,
    candidate_labels,
    hypothesis_template="This abstract is {}."
)

print("ABSTRACT:")
print(abstract)
print("\nAI'S TOP JUDGMENT:")
print(result["labels"][0])
print("\nMODEL SCORE:")
print(round(result["scores"][0], 3))

Stop here and discuss:

  1. What judgment did the model make?
  2. Do you agree?
  3. What words or ideas in the abstract may have influenced the judgment?
  4. Remember: a high score is model confidence, not proof that the judgment is correct.

docs.title: 8. Run the same procedure on ALL abstracts
Code G — Just run this cell
docs.text:
def screen_abstract(text):
    text = str(text)
    result = classifier(
        text,
        candidate_labels,
        hypothesis_template="This abstract is {}."
    )
    top_label = result["labels"][0]

    if top_label.startswith("clearly relevant"):
        return "Clearly relevant"
    elif top_label.startswith("possibly relevant"):
        return "Possibly relevant"
    else:
        return "Probably unrelated"


df["AI Judgment"] = df["abstract"].apply(screen_abstract)

df[["Group Member", "abstract", "AI Judgment"]]

You do not need to understand every line. Read the overall logic:

For each abstract → ask the same model → use the same categories → save the AI judgment.

That is the research idea of systematic repetition.

docs.title: 9. Compare HUMAN vs. AI
docs.text:
Return to the 3 abstracts you personally contributed.

For each one, complete this table:

Group Member Abstract Human Judgment AI Judgment Agree with AI? Reason Alex ... Clearly relevant Clearly relevant Yes The abstract directly studies the exposure and outcome in our question. Maya ... Possibly relevant Probably unrelated No The model may have missed an indirect connection to our outcome.

Your Reason is the most important part. Explain what evidence in the abstract supports your decision.

docs.title: 10. Find ONE interesting disagreement
docs.text:
As a group, choose one case where the human and AI judgments differ—or one case where you almost disagreed.

Be ready to explain:

  • Your research question
  • The human judgment
  • The AI judgment
  • Why the disagreement may have happened
  • What you would do next as the researcher

Possible explanations include:

  • The abstract is genuinely ambiguous
  • Your definition of relevance is too broad or too vague
  • Important information is missing from the abstract
  • The model focused on the wrong words
  • The human reviewer interpreted the research question differently

docs.title: Code H — Run this cell
docs.text:
df.to_csv("week4_ai_results.csv", index=False)
files.download("week4_ai_results.csv")

In plain English: Save the table → download a copy.

docs.title: Assignment 2 Deliverable
docs.text:
Submit one agreement table per group on Blackboard.

Your table should include:

Group Member Abstract Human Judgment AI Judgment Agree with AI? Reason

Each student is responsible for the rows corresponding to the 3 abstracts they personally contributed.

The assignment is about your research judgment, not your ability to memorize Python.

docs.title: If you finish early: optional challenge
docs.text:
Ask your group:

Would you allow this model to automatically EXCLUDE papers from a real literature review? Why or why not?

Think especially about a false exclusion: the AI says a paper is unrelated, but the paper is actually important.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text: AI can assist with repetitive screening. The researcher still defines relevance, checks disagreements, and makes the final decision.

docs.title: Week 9 Day 1: Zoom Research Design Lab
Research Design Sprint
docs.text:
Today’s class is a 20-minute small-group Zoom lab. You will work in a group of 3 to design a small research study from beginning to end.

By the end of the activity, your group should be able to explain:

What do we want to know, who or what will we study, what will we measure or manipulate, and why is our chosen design appropriate?

docs.title: Step 1: Choose a Research Design
docs.text: Your group may choose one of the following:

docs.title: Option A: Survey Study
docs.text:
Use a survey when you want to describe something, compare naturally occurring groups, or examine whether variables are related.

Examples:

  • Is TikTok news use related to perceived news credibility?
  • How often do college students use generative AI for academic work?
  • Do people who follow sports journalists more frequently report greater knowledge of team news?

docs.title: Option B: Randomized Experiment
docs.text:
Use an experiment when you want to test whether manipulating one factor causes a change in an outcome.

Examples:

  • Does adding an AI-generated label to a news post affect perceived credibility?
  • Does a humorous advertisement produce greater purchase intention than a serious advertisement?
  • Does viewing a video apology rather than a written apology affect perceived sincerity?

Remember: an RCT requires random assignment to conditions.

docs.title: Option C: Quasi-Experimental Study
docs.text:
Use a quasi-experiment when you want to examine a possible effect but random assignment is not feasible.

Examples:

  • Does student trust change before and after a university introduces a new AI-use policy?
  • Does a mental-health campaign appear to change attitudes on one campus compared with another campus that did not receive the campaign?
  • Does engagement with a news platform change after the platform introduces a new warning-label policy?

Because participants are not randomly assigned, you must think carefully about alternative explanations.

docs.title: Your 20-Minute Challenge
docs.text:
Choose a topic that interests your group. It can involve journalism, advertising, public relations, social media, sports communication, AI, health communication, entertainment, or another communication-related topic.

Complete the following research design together.

docs.title: 3. Hypothesis — if appropriate
docs.text:
If your group has a reasonable basis for predicting a direction or difference, write a hypothesis. A hypothesis is not required for every study.

H1, if applicable: .................................................................................... ....................................................................................

docs.title: 7. Measurement
docs.text:
How would you actually measure your main outcome?

Be specific. For example, do not only write “trust.” Explain how participants would report or demonstrate trust.

Outcome measure: .................................................................................... ....................................................................................

docs.title: 8–14 Minutes: Build the Design
docs.text: Complete the section that matches your chosen design.

docs.title: If You Chose a Survey
docs.text:
Explain:

  1. How would you recruit participants?
  2. What would participants be asked to report?
  3. What two variables, groups, or outcomes would you compare or relate?
  4. What could you conclude from the results?
  5. What could you not conclude?

Our survey design: .................................................................................... .................................................................................... ....................................................................................

docs.title: If You Chose a Randomized Experiment
If You Chose a Quasi-Experiment
docs.text:
Choose a structure such as:

  • one-group pretest–posttest;
  • nonequivalent comparison group;
  • pretest–posttest with a comparison group; or
  • interrupted time series.

Then explain:

  1. What event, policy, campaign, exposure, or intervention occurs?
  2. Who or what is measured?
  3. When is the outcome measured?
  4. Is there a comparison group?
  5. Why is random assignment not feasible?

Our quasi-experimental design: .................................................................................... .................................................................................... ....................................................................................

docs.title: 14–17 Minutes: Challenge Your Own Study
docs.text:
Every design has limitations.

Identify one major threat, weakness, or alternative explanation in your study.

Examples might include:

  • convenience sampling;
  • poor measurement;
  • self-report bias;
  • selection bias;
  • history;
  • maturation or natural trends;
  • groups differing before the intervention;
  • something other than the treatment differing across experimental conditions.

Our biggest concern: .................................................................................... ....................................................................................

Now identify one realistic improvement.

How we would improve the study: .................................................................................... ....................................................................................

docs.title: 17–20 Minutes: Prepare Your 60-Second Explanation
docs.text:
Your group should be ready to explain your design in approximately 60 seconds.

Use this structure:

We want to know whether/how ____________. We chose a ____________ design because ____________. We would study ____________. Our main predictor/independent variable is ____________, and our outcome is ____________. The main strength of this design is ____________, but one limitation is ____________.

docs.title: Group Roles
docs.text:
With three people, use the following roles to keep the activity moving:

Student 1 — Research Lead Keeps the group focused on the research question and makes sure the design actually answers it.

Student 2 — Design Critic Looks for problems, alternative explanations, weak measurements, or mismatches between the question and the design.

Student 3 — Recorder / Spokesperson Writes the group's final design and prepares the 60-second explanation.

You should still make all major decisions together.

You do not need to run the study or analyze data today. The purpose of this lab is to practice turning a research question into a coherent research design.

docs.title: Week 13 Day 2 — Statistics Zoom Lab
docs.text:
Today: Five groups. Five tests. One short research presentation per group. Each group has its own simulated communication dataset and a ready-to-run Google Colab notebook.

During your 30-minute breakout:

  1. Open your assigned Colab notebook below. The dataset loads automatically; do not download a CSV.
  2. Run the code cells in order (▶). Double-click the YOUR ANSWER text cells and fill in the blanks.
  3. Explain your dataset: What does a row represent? What are your variables? Which are numeric or categorical? Check missing and repeated records.
  4. Explain the research question, run your test, and describe the plot and key result in plain language.
  5. Prepare a 3-minute group presentation: study → variables → plot → statistic + p-value → conclusion. Share your Colab screen.

You are not expected to memorize or write Python code. Work together to understand what the output means. If p ≥ .05, say fail to reject H₀, not “accept H₀.”

docs.title: Your group notebook
docs.text: Group Topic / test Open notebook View dataset (optional) Group 1 Public relations — ANOVA Open Colab View CSV Group 2 Sports journalism — Regression Open Colab View CSV Group 3 Marketing / advertising — Correlation Open Colab View CSV Group 4 Strategic communication — t-test Open Colab View CSV Group 5 Sports journalism — Chi-square Open Colab View CSV

docs.title: Your research question
docs.text:
Group 1 — ANOVA: Does average brand trust differ across three crisis-response styles?

Group 2 — Regression: How does perceived source transparency predict sports story credibility?

Group 3 — Correlation: Are perceived ad relevance and purchase intention related?

Group 4 — t-test: Is average intention to share a public health message different between a facts message and a personal-story message?

Group 5 — Chi-square: Is article clicking (Yes/No) associated with headline style (Neutral/Sensational)?

docs.title: Present to the class
docs.text:
Keep it short. Show one figure or table, state your main result, and explain what the finding does and does not mean. Aim for 3 minutes per group.

All five datasets are simulated for this teaching exercise.

docs.title: Online Books and Course Readings
docs.text:
This course does not rely on a single required textbook. Instead, readings are selected from openly available books, peer-reviewed scholarly articles, research-methods resources, and technical documentation.

Readings are organized around the course's four instructional blocks, progressing from computational and AI literacy to research design, data analysis, and responsible research communication.

Blackboard remains the official source for required readings, weekly preparation instructions, assignment details, and course updates. This page provides a consolidated reference to major course readings and additional resources for review and independent learning.

You are not expected to read every resource listed here in full. Focus on the assigned chapters, sections, and concepts identified in Blackboard announcements.

docs.title: Block 1 — Modern Research Tools in the Age of AI
docs.text:
Weeks 1–5 | Computational Literacy and AI-Assisted Research

The first block introduces the computational environments and AI technologies increasingly used in contemporary research. Students learn foundational concepts behind large language models, Python, and pretrained language models while developing the ability to critically evaluate their use in research workflows.

The goal is computational literacy and methodological judgment, not software engineering or memorizing programming syntax.

docs.title: Research Methods and Computational Social Science
docs.text:
Edelmann, A., Wolff, T., Montagne, D., & Bail, C. A. (2020). Computational Social Science and Sociology.

Annual Review of Sociology, 46, 61–81.

Read the article

This reading introduces how computational methods and digital data are changing social-science research.

Focus on the introduction and the discussion of how computational approaches expand research opportunities while creating methodological challenges.

docs.title: Large Language Models and Transformers
docs.text:
Hugging Face LLM Course

The Hugging Face course provides accessible introductions to natural language processing, Transformers, pretrained language models, and model evaluation.

Assigned introductory sections include:

  • Introduction to Natural Language Processing
  • Introduction to Transformers
  • What Can Transformers Do?
  • How Do Transformers Work?
  • Transformer Architectures

Focus on conceptual understanding rather than mathematical details.

docs.title: Python and Computational Research Environments
docs.text:
Danielle Navarro and Ethan Weed — Learning Statistics with Python

Open Learning Statistics with Python

Assigned introductory sections:

  • Getting Started with Python
  • More Python Concepts

Focus on Python commands, variables, data types, functions, comments, and importing libraries.

Students apply these concepts through guided Google Colab activities.

docs.title: Working with Pretrained Language Models
docs.text:
Hugging Face LLM Course

Assigned sections:

  • Chapter 2 — Introduction
  • Behind the Pipeline
  • Bias and Limitations

These readings support laboratory activities involving pretrained language models and AI-assisted literature screening.

Focus on understanding the basic workflow of using pretrained models, evaluating model-generated classifications, identifying potential bias, and comparing AI outputs with human judgments.

docs.title: Block 2 — Data Collection and Research Design
docs.text:
Weeks 6–8 | Research Questions, Sampling, Measurement, and Research Design

Building on the computational foundation introduced in Block 1, this block focuses on the methodological decisions that determine research quality.

Students learn to formulate research questions and hypotheses, select appropriate research designs, operationalize variables, and evaluate sampling, measurement, and validity.

The emphasis is on understanding why a particular research design is appropriate for a research question, rather than simply identifying different research methods.

docs.title: Sampling Methods in Mass Communication Research
docs.text:
Erba et al. (2018). Sampling Methods and Sample Populations in Quantitative Mass Communication Research Studies: A 15-Year Census of Six Journals.

Communication Research Reports, 35(1), 42–47.

Read the article

Focus on:

  • Probability versus nonprobability sampling
  • Sampling strategies in mass communication research
  • Representativeness
  • Sampling limitations and generalizability

docs.title: Measurement, Reliability, and Validity
docs.text:
Mazer, J. P., & Graham, E. E. (2015). Measurement in Instructional Communication Research: A Decade in Review.

Communication Education, 64(2).

Read the article

Focus on:

  • Measurement decisions
  • Reliability
  • Validity
  • The importance of selecting appropriate measures

docs.title: Survey Research
docs.text:
Navigating Communication Research: A Practical Guide for Media Practitioners

Chapter 7 — Survey Data and Question Design

This introductory resource complements the peer-reviewed readings by explaining survey research in the context of communication and media studies.

Focus on:

  • When surveys are appropriate
  • Survey question design
  • Common measurement approaches
  • Strengths and limitations of survey methods
  • Connections between sampling and survey validity

docs.title: Discrete Choice Experiments
docs.text:
Reynolds et al. (2025). Discrete Choice Experiments: A Primer for the Communication Researcher.

Frontiers in Communication.

Read the article

Focus on the basic logic of experimental research, including:

  • Independent and dependent variables
  • Experimental conditions
  • Manipulation of variables
  • Comparisons between conditions
  • Causal research questions

You may skim more technical sections.

American Journal of Evaluation, 46(1).

Read the article

Research Methods in Psychology — Quasi-Experimental Research

  • Interrupted time-series designs

docs.title: Research Design Review and Application
docs.text:
The research design readings support the Research Design Lab and Assignment 4: Research Design Brief.

Students should be able to explain:

  1. What research question or hypothesis is being investigated?
  2. Who or what is the population of interest, and how will the sample be selected?
  3. What are the major variables, and how will they be measured?
  4. Which research design is most appropriate, and why?
  5. What are the strengths, limitations, and potential validity concerns of the proposed design?

The purpose of this block is to develop sound methodological reasoning before moving into statistical analysis.

docs.title: Block 3 — Data Analysis and Interpretation
docs.text:
Weeks 9–15 | Data Preparation, Statistical Analysis, and Computational Text Analysis

Students apply their computational and research-design knowledge to preparing, analyzing, and interpreting research data.

The emphasis is on understanding the relationship between research questions, variable types, analytical methods, statistical outputs, and substantive interpretation.

docs.title: Learning Statistics with Python
docs.text:
Danielle Navarro and Ethan Weed

Open Learning Statistics with Python

This is the primary introductory statistics resource used throughout Block 3.

Selected sections support:

  • Data preparation and data wrangling
  • Descriptive statistics
  • Data visualization
  • Hypothesis testing
  • Independent-samples t-tests
  • Correlation
  • Linear regression
  • ANOVA
  • Chi-square tests

Students are not expected to read the entire book or memorize mathematical derivations. Focus on the sections assigned through Blackboard.

docs.title: Data Structure, Cleaning, and Preparation
docs.text:
Learning Statistics with Python

  • Chapter 1 — Why Do We Learn Statistics?
  • Chapter 7 — Data Wrangling
  • Section 7.1 — DataFrames
  • Section 7.2 — Tabulating and Cross-Tabulating Data

Open the book

Focus on understanding how data are structured and prepared before conducting statistical analyses.

In guided Google Colab activities, students practice:

  • Inspecting datasets
  • Identifying missing or problematic values
  • Working with DataFrames
  • Producing descriptive summaries
  • Cross-tabulating variables
  • Creating basic visualizations

docs.title: Comparing Two Means: t-Tests
docs.text:
Learning Statistics with Python — Comparing Two Means

Focus on the independent-samples t-test.

Key concepts include:

  • Comparing the means of two groups
  • Identifying appropriate independent and dependent variables
  • Understanding the null hypothesis
  • Interpreting test statistics and p-values
  • Explaining findings in substantive terms

docs.title: Correlation and Linear Regression
docs.text:
Learning Statistics with Python

Assigned topics:

  • Correlation
  • Linear Regression

For correlation, focus on the introductory concepts in Section 5.6.

Key concepts include:

  • Positive and negative associations
  • Correlation coefficients
  • Scatterplots
  • Predictor and outcome variables
  • The basic interpretation of a regression line
  • Understanding why correlation does not establish causation

Students use Python to conduct introductory analyses and interpret results.

docs.title: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
docs.text:
Learning Statistics with Python — Chapter 15: Comparing Several Means

Focus particularly on:

  • Section 15.1 — An Illustrative Data Set
  • Section 15.2 — How ANOVA Works
  • Conducting and interpreting one-way ANOVA

The central research question is:

How can we determine whether a numerical outcome differs across more than two groups?

Students should understand:

  • When ANOVA is appropriate
  • Between-group and within-group variation
  • The F-statistic
  • Statistical significance
  • Interpretation of group differences

Detailed mathematical derivations may be skimmed.

docs.title: Chi-Square Tests
docs.text:
Learning Statistics with Python — Chapter 13: Categorical Data Analysis

Assigned sections:

  • Section 13.2 — The Chi-Square Test of Independence or Association
  • Section 13.2.2 — Doing the Test in Python

Focus on the chi-square test of independence rather than the goodness-of-fit test.

Key concepts include:

  • Categorical variables
  • Contingency tables
  • Observed and expected frequencies
  • Testing associations between categorical variables
  • Interpreting chi-square results

docs.title: Connecting Statistical Models
docs.text:
Students review the relationships among:

  • Independent-samples t-tests
  • One-way ANOVA
  • Linear regression

This session emphasizes how different statistical methods can be understood within a broader framework of analytical reasoning.

No additional reading is required beyond the previously assigned statistical materials.

docs.title: Computational Text Analysis and Sentiment Classification
docs.text:
Hugging Face LLM Course

Transformers: What Can They Do?

Focus on the discussion of pipelines and the sentiment-analysis example.

Students examine the basic computational workflow:

Text → Pretrained Model → Classification → Score

The reading introduces the use of pipeline("sentiment-analysis") to classify text and produce a prediction score.

In Google Colab, students implement and evaluate a similar workflow while considering model limitations and the interpretation of classification outputs.

docs.title: How to Approach Block 3 Readings
docs.text:
You are not expected to memorize formulas or Python syntax.

For each statistical method, focus on four questions:

  1. What kind of research question does this method answer?
  2. What types of variables does it use?
  3. What does the Python output tell us?
  4. How can the result be explained in plain language?

The lectures and Google Colab notebooks provide guided practice with the analytical workflows students are expected to understand.

docs.title: Block 4 — Responsible Research and Communication
docs.text:
Week 16 | Research Ethics, Reproducibility, and Communication

The final block integrates the methodological and analytical knowledge developed throughout the semester.

Topics include:

  • Research ethics
  • Responsible AI use
  • Research validity and limitations
  • Reproducibility
  • Interpretation and communication of research findings
  • Translating analytical findings for academic, industry, and other stakeholder audiences

Students apply these principles through their final research projects and presentations.

Specific readings or preparation materials, when assigned, will be communicated through Blackboard.

docs.title: Generative AI
docs.text:
Selected generative AI tools may be used for course activities involving:

  • Coding assistance
  • Debugging
  • Research organization
  • Classification support
  • Methodological critique
  • Understanding computational workflows

The specific tools may vary as AI technologies and access conditions evolve.

AI use is assignment-specific and must follow the instructions provided by the instructor.

Students are responsible for verifying AI-assisted work, explaining their analytical decisions, and maintaining academic integrity.

The emphasis is not simply on obtaining an AI-generated answer, but on evaluating the output, recognizing limitations, and maintaining human oversight.

Never upload confidential, personally identifiable, restricted, or otherwise sensitive data to external AI systems or computational platforms without appropriate authorization.

docs.title: Research and Scholarly Resources
docs.text:
Depending on the research question and activity, students may also use:

  • University library databases
  • Peer-reviewed scholarly journals
  • Communication research-methods references
  • Statistical consulting resources
  • Academic writing support resources
  • Accessibility resources
  • Official technical documentation

When conducting literature-based research, prioritize original peer-reviewed studies and evaluate the relevance, credibility, and methodological quality of sources.

AI-generated summaries should not replace independent evaluation of scholarly literature.

docs.title: Getting Technical Help
docs.text:
Debugging is a normal part of computational research.

When requesting technical help from the instructor, classmates, documentation, or an authorized AI coding assistant, try to provide:

  1. Your objective — What are you trying to accomplish?
  2. The relevant data — What variables or data structure are involved?
  3. Your code — What did you run?
  4. The error — What happened?
  5. Your expectation — What did you expect to happen?
  6. What you already tried — What changes or solutions have you tested?

Providing this information makes it easier to diagnose problems and helps you develop a systematic, reproducible approach to computational problem-solving.

When sharing code, error messages, or sample data, remove confidential or personally identifiable information.
